questions.q: Which three drivers does the lesson say actually fund real governance programs?
questions.explain: The lesson frames every funded governance program as serving compliance, trust, value, or some combination of the three.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say compliance is the easiest driver to get budget for?
options: Compliance never requires any organizational change
It is the cheapest driver to implement
The cost of ignoring it is explicit and legal, with real financial penalties
questions.explain: Regulations like GDPR carry explicit, large financial penalties, making the cost of non-compliance concrete and easy to justify funding against.

questions.q: What specific, visible symptom does the lesson identify as a sign of low data trust?
options: People quietly rebuilding their own version of a report because they don't trust the official one
A sudden increase in data storage costs
questions.explain: Low trust shows up as duplicated effort — shadow versions of reports — rather than as an obvious, logged governance complaint.

questions.q: How does the lesson frame value-driven governance differently from compliance-driven governance?
options: Value-driven governance only applies to regulated industries
Value-driven governance is always funded before compliance work
Value-driven governance is pitched as an enabler that lets the business move faster, not just a way to avoid risk
Value-driven governance has no measurable outcome at all
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts 'stop bad things from happening' (compliance/risk framing) with 'good data lets the business move faster' (value framing).

questions.q: Per the lesson, which regulation specifically applies to health data in the United States?
questions.explain: HIPAA governs health data in the US; GDPR and CPRA are EU and California privacy laws respectively, and ISO 38505 is a data governance standard, not a health-data law.
